title: Compressed air and nitrogen
calcLabel: Read the compressed air and nitrogen guide
ends: The utilities bill just went down.

steps.q: Of the electricity a compressor uses, roughly how much ends up as useful work at the air tool?
board: how much ends up as useful
steps.title: Costly air
steps.summary: Compressing air turns most of the motor's power into heat, and leaks, pressure drops and over-pressure waste more, so only about 10 % ends up as useful work. Avoid using compressed air for jobs a fan or blower can do, and fix leaks first, since plants often lose a fifth or more of their air through them.

steps.q: You lower the compressor discharge pressure by 1 bar. Roughly what power saving?
steps.title: Pressure costs power
steps.summary: Compression power rises with the pressure ratio, so around a typical 7 bar, each 1 bar reduction saves roughly 6 to 8 % of compressor power, and leaks fall too. If one user needs higher pressure, serve it with a local booster rather than running the whole system high.

steps.q: Why does instrument air need a low dew point?
steps.title: Dry air
steps.summary: Compressed air carries water vapour that condenses as the air cools in the lines, causing rust, blocked positioner ports and sticking valves. Instrument air is dried to a dew point below the coldest temperature it will meet, often around −40 °C. Check the dryer and drain receivers and filters regularly.

steps.q: You ask a PSA nitrogen plant for 99.99 % purity instead of 99 %. What happens to its output?
steps.title: Purity costs
steps.summary: A PSA nitrogen generator holds oxygen back on an adsorbent bed and lets nitrogen through. Higher purity means less of the air leaves as product, so raising purity from 99 % to 99.99 % can roughly halve the output from the same compressor. Specify the purity each user really needs; blanketing and purging often manage with 98 to 99 %.

draw: match purity to the real need

steps.q: A vessel was purged with nitrogen. Someone has to go inside. What must be checked?
steps.title: Nitrogen kills quietly
steps.summary: Nitrogen is colourless and odourless and displaces oxygen; a few breaths of nitrogen-rich air can cause collapse without warning. Before entry, isolate and blind the nitrogen and every other line, ventilate with air, confirm oxygen of at least 19.5 % and test for flammable and toxic gas with a calibrated meter, recorded on the entry permit. Keep a standby person outside, monitor continuously, and never attempt rescue without breathing apparatus.

opts.t: Oxygen, by test, on a permit
That the nitrogen valve is shut

steps.q: Can you use compressed air to pressure-transfer a flammable solvent?
steps.title: Never air
steps.summary: Compressed air brings 21 % oxygen into a solvent's vapour space, creating a flammable mixture that static from the flow or any spark can ignite. Use nitrogen for pressure transfers and blanketing, within the vessel's pressure rating, and use different couplings for air and nitrogen hoses, as well as labels, so they cannot be swapped.

opts.t: Only if a pump isn't available
Yes, if the air is dry

draw: different couplings for air and N₂

intro.text: Hi, I'm Bubbles. Today: compressed air and nitrogen. Invisible, everywhere, and expensive. Six questions. Ready?

outro-web.text: That's the lesson. Read the compressed air and nitrogen guide next.

q1.text: Question 1. Of the electricity a compressor uses, roughly how much ends up as useful work at the air tool?

q1-r0.text: About 10 percent. The rest is mostly heat.

q1-r1.text: Far too generous. Most of it leaves as heat.

q1-r2.text: If only. Compressed air is one of the costliest utilities.

q1-r3.text: No machine is that good, least of all an air compressor.

q1-b0.text: Compressing air makes heat. Most of the motor's power leaves in the cooling water or air.

q1-b1.text: Then leaks, pressure drops and over-pressure waste more. Only about a tenth does useful work.

q1-b2.text: So never use compressed air for cooling people, drying floors or blowing dust. A fan or a blower costs far less.

q1-b3.text: Fix leaks first. A plant can lose a fifth or more of its air through leaks nobody hears.

q2.text: Question 2. You lower the compressor discharge pressure by 1 bar. Roughly what power saving?

q2-r0.text: Too small. Each bar costs a lot more than that.

q2-r2.text: Too much for one bar. Nice dream though.

q2-r3.text: Lower pressure always takes less power to make.

q2-b0.text: Compression power rises with the pressure ratio. Every extra bar costs.

q2-b1.text: Around the usual 7 bar, each bar less saves roughly 6 to 8 percent.

q2-b2.text: Leaks drop too, because a hole leaks less at lower pressure.

q2-b3.text: Go only as low as the most demanding user truly needs, then give any single high user a booster. Don't run the whole plant high for it.

q3.text: Question 3. Why does instrument air need a low dew point?

q3-r0.text: Dew point has nothing to do with pressure delivered.

q3-r1.text: Yes! Wet air means rust, blocked ports and sticking valves.

q3-r2.text: Oil is a filter's job. Dew point is about water.

q3-r3.text: It matters a lot. Ask anyone with a stuck valve.

q3-b0.text: Compressed air holds water vapour. As it cools in the lines, the water condenses.

q3-b1.text: Water rusts pipes, blocks small ports in positioners, and makes valves stick.

q3-b2.text: Dry it to a pressure dew point below the coldest the air will ever see. Instrument air is often dried to about minus 40 degrees.

q3-b3.text: Check the dryer regularly, and drain the receivers and filters. Their drains fail quietly.

q4.text: Question 4. You ask a PSA nitrogen plant for 99.99 % purity instead of 99 %. What happens to its output?

q4-r0.text: Higher purity takes more air per cubic metre of nitrogen.

q4-r1.text: Purity has a big price in output.

q4-r3.text: It still runs, just with much less gas.

q4-b0.text: A PSA plant holds oxygen back on a sieve bed and lets nitrogen through.

q4-b1.text: The purer you want the nitrogen, the less of the air comes out as product.

q4-b2.text: Going from 99 to 99.99 percent can cut the output to around half, for the same compressor.

q4-b3.text: Specify what each user really needs, and check the oxygen limit for each use. Blanketing and purging often manage with 98 to 99 percent.

q5.text: Question 5. A vessel was purged with nitrogen. Someone has to go inside. What must be checked?

q5-r0.text: Cool helps, but nitrogen can kill at any temperature.

q5-r1.text: Yes! At least 19.5 percent, tested, on a permit, and watched.

q5-r2.text: Necessary, but not enough on its own.

q5-r3.text: Nitrogen can kill in a few breaths with no warning.

q5-b0.text: Nitrogen has no colour or smell. It pushes out the oxygen, and a few breaths can knock a person out.

q5-b1.text: Before entry: isolate and blind the nitrogen and every other line, ventilate with air, and test the atmosphere.

q5-b2.text: Oxygen must be at least 19.5 percent, and flammable and toxic gas readings must be clear, all by a calibrated meter on the entry permit.

q5-b3.text: Keep a standby person outside, and monitor continuously. Never go in to rescue without breathing apparatus.

q6.text: Question 6. Can you use compressed air to pressure-transfer a flammable solvent?

q6-r0.text: Even then, air brings 21 percent oxygen into the vapour space. Use nitrogen.

q6-r1.text: Correct! Air plus solvent vapour is a fire waiting for a spark.

q6-r2.text: Dry air still has 21 percent oxygen.

q6-r3.text: Low pressure still makes a flammable vapour space.

q6-b0.text: Air brings 21 percent oxygen into the solvent's vapour space. Now it's a flammable mixture.

q6-b1.text: Static from the flow, or any spark, can ignite it.

q6-b2.text: Use nitrogen for pressure transfers and blanketing, and check the vessel's pressure rating.

q6-b3.text: Use different couplings for air and nitrogen, so the hoses can't be swapped, and label them too. More in the compressed air and nitrogen guide on pharmacheme dot in.
